Mr. Speaker, last evening before the house adjourned I began speaking in support of the Social Credit amendment regretting the failure of the government to bring before the house for adoption a realistic financial system, which kind of financial system might be defined as one capable of making that which is physically possible in a nation financially possible. Of course our present system cannot possibly do that. I quoted, from eminent present-day official authorities, statements that indicate clearly that a world economic crisis is in the making. They indicate also that our main problem in the world is a monetary problem.
I deplored the fact that mankind appeared so fearful of doing anything real to reform our present monetary system, so unwilling even to discuss intelligently what Sir Basil Blackett characterized in 1931 as "the insanity of the monetary system with which man has tortured himself ever since he passed from barter to money."
For an example of the insanity and the torture, take the great depression in the United States. Between the years 1929 and 1934 money in circulation in that nation decreased in quantity from $23 billion to $15 billion. That amount of money, $8 billion, was actually withdrawn from circulation in that country. The great depression accompanied that $8 billion withdrawal with all its concomitant loss, unemployment and suffering.
As another example, take Canada. Between the years 1929 and 1934 $932 million were withdrawn in our nation-and the great depression was on us! I should like to ask whoever consider themselves to be the wisest two men in the Conservative party, so far as money is concerned, to tell me whether they have any idea what the Conservatives would do if a similar state of affairs were to begin to arise in Canada today, and they were in power. I should like the two wisest men in the Liberal party to tell us what they would do.

I can get you many of them.
Why did the war eliminate the depression? Well, in the first place, it limited the production of consumer goods. We were told all through the depression that we had overproduction. All hon. members of the house will recall that statement. It was not underconsumption they thought, it was overproduction. Well, that sounds foolish now, doesn't it? It did not seem to sound foolish to some, however, for they went serenely on deluding themselves and all who listened to them; but the war limited production of consumer goods and concentrated the nation's efforts towards producing war materials. At the same time we distributed throughout the nation the money spent for producing war materials, and that money was used to buy the consumer goods which were not previously going into circulation. That began to improve conditions from the standpoint of prosperity.
The war provided employment for the unemployed-both in the armed forces and in war production. There is no one, even in the Liberal party, who will question that.
We distributed great quantities of money out among the people by means of various payments that were made in the carrying on of the war. Those are the things that brought Canada out of the depression, and when any one of our good Liberal friends thinks he can refute those statements he can take a full period and I will listen to him with great pleasure. I know that he cannot do it.
How could that withdrawal of $8 billion from circulation in the United States have been prevented? How could it have been


overcome? I will let any man here ask himself that. I know that the members of this house are all honourable members and good men, but-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Thank you.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Let every member here ask himself pointedly what he would have done if he had been the president of the United States in 1930 and had seen that withdrawal taking place. What would he have done to remedy it if he had been the president of the United States with full power in 1935? What would he have done to overcome the difficulty, to bring back into circulation that $8 billion? When he can answer that question he is ready to begin to get wisdom concerning these matters.
Meanwhile, notice that the depression in both Canada and the United States was a monetary problem. When the money went out of circulation unemployment developed. People were not able to buy goods. The price of goods went down-mainly on primary production-and all those other terrible things occurred which characterized that depression.
I will ask that same question of hon. members again. I indicated that I would not -single out any particular member as it might embarrass him, but I will ask anybody in the house to answer the question:	How would
you have put that money back into circulation in Canada? How would you have prevented it from going out of circulation?
Why did it go out of circulation? Because the bankers, who are the only ones who lend money, lost confidence and began to withdraw their loans, and refused to advance further loans. How would you have stopped that? How-with your present outmoded and ineffective monetary system, which as I said a moment ago may be characterized as insane?
May we go back in history and take the United States in 1918? This incident is one of the main causes of the problems with which we find ourselves confronted in the world today. Before 1914 the United States was a debtor country. She was worrying almost as much as we now are about how her trade balance could be kept favourable. After 1918 she was very greatly industrialized because the United States had been called upon to be the workshop of the allied world to produce supplies for the fighting forces. She had tremendously developed her productive capacity, and when the war was over she did not know where in the world she could sell the surplus goods that she was able to produce. That was the beginning of the troubles which are torturing us today.

If you had been the president of the United States in those days what would you have done? The United States found that she had $60 billion worth of goods in the country and only $45 billion worth of money placed into circulation with which to buy those goods. Now, what would you have done if you had been president with full power? When you can answer that you are in a position to begin to discuss intelligently modern economic problems.
The United States actually did two things. First of all, she began a system of lending abroad. She lent money in Europe and in other countries so that they might buy her surplus goods. As long as she was able to keep that money going over there into those countries they would buy her surplus and she was able to keep the wheels of her industry running and her people employed. Just as soon as she discovered that she was no longer able to afford those loans abroad-in 1928 and in 1929-trouble immediately began to fall upon her. With the rest of the world she took us down into a depression.
There are a good many members honouring me with careful attention. In order to justify what I say I will suggest that they read the book "The United States in the World Economy", which explains all this very simply and does not involve Liberals, Conservatives or any others. It just tells what happened.
Then the United States, in 1922, instituted the unconditional most-favoured-nation clause. By this she put the nations into an economic strait-jacket which helped to bring on the depression. No one can understand the conditions that we are living in today unless he understands that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You tell them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would be glad to tell them. In fact, I gave several speeches last session on this very subject.
What would you have done, I ask again, if you had been president of the United States? Would you have done as the United States did or would you have tried a financial system whereby you could have put purchasing power into the hands of people and enabled them to buy your surplus goods?
The United States could not do that with the unsound system she had then and has now because all the money she gets into circulation has to be borrowed. She cannot get money into circulation until someone will lend it. There is the trouble with our present system.
Socialism would say "Well, we would redistribute." I ask the socialists and all the rest who are listening: How in the world
The Address-Mr. Blackmcre could you redistribute $45 billion of money to make it buy $60 billion of goods? I just ask the question to show the absolute absurdity of a proposal of redistributing wealth to solve this problem.
Then, there are those who will say "Trade". Anyone who says that the United States was not doing everything possible to trade, just does not know much about the subject. She was doing everything in her power, "blasting her way into the world's markets" in a manner far superior to anything R. B. Bennett ever tried. She was constantly in danger of an adverse trade balance even when she did try to trade.
What did the United States actually do? I have indicated that she used two devices. She started foreign lending which she obviously could not keep up as long as she was lending debt money; and instituted the unconditional most-favoured-nation clause in 1922. The fundamental principle which underlies the unconditional most-favoured-nation clause is the principle of non-discrimination, of which our leaders in this country apparently have now become utterly and fanatically enamoured.
This is where modern talk of the principle of non-discrimination began. Actually it means the very worst kind of discrimination, especially against the weaker economies. Ultimately this policy caused other nations to resort to exchange controls, quotas, high tariffs, attempts to barter and attempts to set up reciprocal tariff arrangements, all of which the United States ignorantly termed economic aggression. The United States designed the Bretton Woods agreement to prevent "economic aggression," as she called it, but did not do one single thing about adjusting this disequilibrium that had grown up, illustrated by the figures of that $60 billion of goods in her possession with only $45 billion of money in circulation to buy the goods.
This whole set-up ultimately precipitated a war. I say once more to the people in the country who will read my remarks, whether anyone in this house will listen, and I am not saying they are not doing it: unless we understand these facts we are not beginning to have the wisdom to understand those quotations which I put on the record last night.
The question will be asked, what would Social Credit have done? Social Credit is eager to tell. People who do not know "shucks" about it are ready to tell all about it. People who do not understand these great fundamental problems are quick to say that Social Credit will not work. That is utter nonsense. Men become blind leaders of the
550	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Blackmore blind when they carry on as some members have done here, particularly some of the members from British Columbia.
Social Credit would, first of all, introduce a realistic financial system, one which would make what is physically possible financially possible. Now, on the face of it, is that not exactly what you would want? If, in the United States, there were $60 billion worth of goods and only $45 billion worth of money, the first thing was to make financially possible the purchase of those goods which it was physically possible to produce. The government of the United States did not do that; and that is what caused all the trouble.
Social Credit would introduce a monetary system employing money based upon goods and services and not upon gold, either directly or indirectly. I believe that practically every member in this house would agree with that if he were free to talk about the matter. Social Credit would set up a monetary commission, the business of which would be to see that money came into circulation directly in accordance with the needs of business, both for producing and for distributing goods and services. One of the difficulties with all the orthodox thinking men is that they are ready to issue money in accordance with the needs of business for producing, but not for consuming, for distributing. Distributing in this case means the effecting of exchanges of goods and services to the extent necessary to enable all of the people to enjoy the products of the nation's resources to the optimum desirable degree of production. There is nothing wrong with that on the face of it, is there?
This monetary commission would take counsel with the banks and other lending institutions in the nation and, where necessary, would aid them, to the end that every deserving prospective producer of desired goods and services be afforded financial credit to enable him to produce adequately. There is no one who will object to that, but they do not know how to do it under the present system.
Moreover, this monetary commission would . create dollars and issue them debt-free in such ways, and to such people, and in such amounts, as to enable people to consume the otherwise not consumable portion of the nation's production, or such goods as the appropriate portion of that production might be traded abroad for. I do not think anyone will question the advisability of that, but they do not know how to do it. It cannot be done without debt-free money.
Social Credit would adopt measures adequate for the establishment and maintenance of a just price to producers, comprising the


cost of production plus a fair profit. I think no one will object to that. The question is, how to do it. It cannot be done without debt-free money.
Social Credit would, through the monetary commission, issue to consumers consumer purchasing power in such forms and in such amounts as might be found needful to equate consumption with production in the nation's economy. That sounds sensible, does it not? It cannot be done without debt-free money. Such issues of consumer purchasing power might fittingly be called national dividends.
Now, the financial system-

The financial system I have outlined would render what is physically possible in the nation's economy financially possible. Any financial system not comprising the principles and the techniques I have outlined cannot possibly render financially possible what is physically possible.
The question everyone asks is, would such dollars, created by the commission and issued debt-free, be sound? We hear a lot of silly talk about "rubber" dollars and "funny" money. These statements are based on lack of knowledge and understanding, that is all. That is the kindest thing I can say.
Could the principle of issuing such money be sound? There is one statement on this matter by the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, in his report appearing in the Times, of January 30, 1936. His statement reads:
Additional currency, however, can now be furnished by the authorities, if they choose to exercise their powers without reference to the central bank's holding of gold. Thus the nineteenth century, which brought into general use a means of payment hitherto scarcely known outside London, brought also the machinery whereby it could be subjected to intelligent control.
We learnt that a shortage of money may be just as vicious in its effects as an excess, though deflation has still a touch of virtue about it in the minds of many people. Nevertheless it is becoming more and more widely recognized that greater productivity calls for an increased supply of money, for otherwise prices will fall, business will stagnate, and the growing productive capacity will be unused.
For money to be truly "sound" there must be enough of it to finance an ordinarily growing volume of trade, yet not so much as to give rise to an inflationary movement of prices.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, it is absolutely impossible to provide that extra money about which the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna talked, except through the creation and employment of debt-free money. It is

unquestionable that the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna had in mind creating money not based on gold.
Now, what about the Bradbury experiment in Great Britain during world war I?
Now, what would you do about-
I shall answer all your questions later. This whole experiment is well described in "Currency, Credit and the Exchanges" by Dr. William A. Shaw, published in 1926.
What about the gold mines in British Columbia?

Dr. Shaw is the editor of the Calendar of Treasury Records at Her Majesty's public records office. I discussed this whole matter on June 7, 1951.
Dr. William A. Shaw in 1930 published a book entitled "The Theory and Principles of Central Banking". At page 50 of this book he discusses the Bradbury experiment with great admiration. At page 51 he uses the following words:
After ten years of illuminating experience this perfect, uncontrolled, and uncontrollable automatic currency system was thrown over, the automatic principle was surrendered, and our currency, although declared by law to be inconvertible paper, was placed (or was supposed to be placed) under the control of the Bank of England, and became once again sensitive (or was supposed to be made sensitive) to the vagaries of a fluctuating gold cover fund.
Why was this retrograde step taken, and why did England thus throw over the pure theory of currency issue, which she had accidentally discovered and so wonderfully exemplified to the world?
All those who wish to call Social Credit proposals "funny money" had better consider the opinions of Dr. William A. Shaw, one of the world's greatest authorities. There is no sufficient reason why state money like the Bradbury could not be issued and "spent" into circulation, debt-free.
How much money can be safely created and issued debt-free? The amount depends exactly upon the unpurchased surplus of goods in the nation's economy, and unused productive capacity as regards consumers' goods. That is the answer the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) wanted a few days ago.

Mr. Speaker, I venture to divert the attention of the house this afternoon to another subject which I hope hon. members will find as important and
The Address-Mr. Graydon perhaps, in some respects, as interesting, as some of the other subjects which have been discussed during this debate. I take part in this debate largely because this fall I was again privileged to be a part of the Canadian delegation to the seventh general assembly of the United Nations. As the minister has given a somewhat comprehensive review of some of the matters which were dealt with at that general assembly, I thought I should say a word about the gathering, viewing it from the position of a parliamentary observer.
We were meeting this fall in new headquarters which were both ornate and highly modern in their appointments. They had a somewhat peaceful setting. I only wish that peaceful setting in greater measure reflected world conditions as we found them represented by the various nations there.
As one goes into the new structure, one finds the seven Canadian doors, made of Canadian nickel, through which the public passes into the United Nations meeting place, and which were the gift of the people of Canada. In the plenary session of the general assembly and in its committee formations one finds many of our Canadians operating there. One finds there, for the first time as the president of this world organization, our own Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and with him, as chairman of the delegation, one finds the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), and also the hon. member for Huron-Perth (Mr. McLean), the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne), who is in the house this afternoon, and Senator Isnor from the other place. When one finds there those Canadians, together with others who are taking part in the delegation work, both as staff, advisers and in other capacities, one feels very much at home at the United Nations these days.
While I was there I was interested in reminiscing on the changes which have taken place since the San Francisco conference. As a matter of fact I think there were there on this occasion at the first part of this general assembly only two of us who represented Canada at the San Francisco conference some seven years ago. Use of force is advocated by C.C.F. coast leader. Harold Winch tells audience here change is coming in Canada "peacefully or not"

In your own speeches.

People shout at us that this is socialism, bolshevism. Maybe it is. What of it?

Oh, oh.

International communism is a policy, a movement; international finance is a policy, a movement; international political Zionism is a policy, a movement; and I was opposed to all three at that time. I linked them together because there was plenty of evidence-and I have that evidence and can produce it at the proper time-
The time is now.

These three great movements had deliberately plotted to destroy Britain's attempts to exercise the mandate in Israel as she was supposed to. Mr. Speaker, when one intervenes for the second time in a debate I feel that perhaps a word of explanation or even apology is necessary. My apology is that I wish to refer to an incident which, though it concerns one individual primarily, I think concerns us all because I firmly believe it is a matter where gross injustice has been done through political interference. I refer to the case of Robert Pitt of the Fort Garry hotel, Winnipeg. I shall try now to satisfy the house that what 1 have said is true, and that no reasonable man can come to any other conclusion on an examination of the facts.
Mr. Pitt himself has kept silent; therefore I am confined entirely to and I rely entirely on what has appeared in the press. I believe everything I shall quote from the press is from the Winnipeg Tribune. I believe there are a lot of people in this house who are in a position to say-though the Tribune does not need any endorsement of this kind-of their own knowledge that what the Tribune says is true.
On September 10 last the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and a party visited the Fort Garry hotel. Approximately two months later the manager of the hotel, an old and valued servant of the Canadian National hotel system, was sent from the Fort Garry hotel in Winnipeg to the Prince Edward hotel in Brandon. Now, it is interesting that the report which appeared in the Tribune was brought to that newspaper through the instrumentality of the hotel workers. The phrase used by the Tribune is that a spokesman for the Fort Garry hotel employees gave them the information which they set out. I think that has special significance. I shall have other things to say to indicate the quality of Mr. Pitt, but I think it is of some significance that the men who had worked under him-incidentally it is pointed out that he had substantially reduced the staff of the hotel, so it looks as if he had perhaps not always done things that the union wanted him to do-give this account which is produced by the Tribune.
I should add that this was not a formal statement on behalf of the union. Lest I forget later, I might read here what the union said on that point. Officials of the union
The Address-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell denied that their organization charged that there was political interference in Mr. Pitt's demotion. This is what they say:
Although staff members intended, protesting the C.N.R. decision, even though it is a managerial problem, they now feel the airing of the situation in the Tribune makes this move unnecessary.
I read from a report in the Tribune, which is dated November 13:
But hotel employees today listed two specific incidents for which they allege Mr. Pitt was called on the carpet.
The first is "that the Prime Minister and his party were not properly received at the hotel rotunda". This newspaper explains the scene exactly as it happened, and I think it is very easy for us to picture that. I quote again from the newspaper:
At the time the party entered the hotel, Mr. St. Laurent was surrounded by a group of young Liberals who had met him at the C.N.R. station at 11 a.m. They headed directly for the elevator through the crowded lobby, making it difficult for Mr. Pitt, who was standing in the lobby, to approach and welcome the Prime Minister.
Now then, the second complaint is "that there were no rooms immediately available for all the members of the party". Reservations had been requested the previous day.
I do not know which of these two complaints is the most trivial and childish. I think we can picture the scene; the Prime Minister entering the hotel and being surrounded by his supporters, of which he has no doubt a considerable number in Winnipeg. They surrounded him and were with him until he took the elevator to go to his quarters.
The only possible way one could imagine any failure on Mr. Pitt's part, the only thing I can suggest is in itself a nonsensical thing. The complaint apparently might be that Mr. Pitt did not force his way through the group in order to present himself to the Prime Minister; a sort of bucking the line technique.
The second complaint is perhaps of a slightly stronger character. It was that there were no rooms immediately available for all members of the party. Here perhaps we find something which we can understand better. Here we may find some very important personages, at least in their own minds, who take themselves very seriously and who may have fancied that they had not been treated with all the deference to which they considered themselves entitled. The report makes it clear that the reservations had been requested only the day before. In a busy hotel like this, we all know you cannot always count on getting your reservations on such short notice. I can only imagine some of these people, as I say, were aggrieved. It is stated, as I shall point out later, that the

Shakespeare has words for it:

Drest in a little brief authority,
Most ignorant of what he's most assured, . . . Plays such fantastic tricks before high heaven As make the angels weep.
There you have this picture in Winnipeg on September 10. Two months later comes the word to Mr. Pitt that he is to go to the Prince Edward hotel in Brandon.
I now want to draw your attention for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to this man's career in the hotel business, in the employment of the Canadian National hotels. He was the manager of the Nova Scotian at Halifax from December 8, 1931 to November 1, 1941, practically ten years. I am reading now from the answer I received from the Department of Transport. Then he went into the army and was in the army for several years, in the armoured corps-losing his eye, incidentally, during the war-but came back, was able to resume his duties and was manager of the Bessborough at Saskatoon from August 15, 1946 to July 12, 1951 when he was transferred to the Fort Garry. Does anyone imagine that a man who had served for that length of time in that capacity would not know how to treat a Prime Minister or would not know how to treat appropriately the other people who were with the Prime Minister? Of all the requirements that a hotel manager must meet, I suggest that probably that the proper treatment of his guests stands out above all the rest.
Are we to assume that this man, with this experience, who is taken back after his army service and who goes from one large hotel to another; are we to believe for one moment that these childish suggestions could apply to him? I cannot believe that. I do not think anyone in this house can believe it. Nevertheless according to this record which, as I say, came from the labour people, he was demoted for that reason. I regret to say that the president of the Canadian National Railways gave a different reason. I regret that Mr. Gordon, for whom I have immense respect, gave this reason because I cannot accept it and I do not believe anyone in this house can accept it. What he says is this:
Changes in management affecting several hotels follow normal reviews of hotel operations that are carried out by the general manager of hotels.


In other words we are apparently asked to believe that this man who had been manager of the Nova Scotian hotel, with 150 rooms, for 10 years-

speechtext: He was never manager of the Nova Scotian hotel.*
I am reading now from the answer I received from the Department of Transport, which one likes to assume is correct.
Or partially correct, anyway.

I read:
He was manager of the Nova Scotian at Halifax from December 8, 1931 to November 1, 1941.
If that is wrong I wish the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) would tell the Department of Transport that it is wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will speak about this matter a little bit later.

All right. He was manager of the Nova Scotian, according to the Department of Transport, for 10 years, leaving it to go into the army. He then went to the Bessborough hotel, a hotel with 260 rooms; and according to the Department of Transport-which apparently may be wrong -he was appointed on August 15, 1946, and there is nothing to indicate that there was any gap there. From this I assume that, when he went, on July 12, 1951, to the Fort Garry, he went from the Bessborough.
How many rooms has the Bessborough?

The Bessborough has 260 rooms; and he is now sent from a hotel with 260 rooms to a hotel with 80 rooms. Yet we are asked to believe that this is normal procedure. If it is normal procedure, all I can suggest is that the Canadian National Railways business is carried on in an abnormal way, something which I do not believe. It is no wonder that the Winnipeg Tribune reports as follows:
Of those contacted by the Tribune today-
That was November 14.
-none accepted C.N.R. president Donald Gordon's explanation of Mr. Pitt's transfer to a lesser post, which was announced on Wednesday.
I do not wonder that nobody accepted it, because no reasonable men would accept it.
I wish now to refer briefly to the answers I received from the Department of Transport to the questions which I asked. The first one to which I wish to refer is this. I am not reading all the answers because some of them are just references to the
See amended statement on page 579.

facts of his service with the railway company. However, I asked this question:
Had there been any complaint regarding his work there?
That was at the Fort Garry hotel. The answer is "Yes". I believe that is an unworthy answer, because there is a great deal of evidence-and I shall read some of it in a moment-to show that he was a highly efficient man. The fact that he held these various appointments showed that during all those years the railway certainly thought that he was efficient. I believe this answer is either inaccurate or that it refers to some very trivial matter. Of course it is conceivable that it refers to the complaint to which I am taking objection. It is conceivable that it refers to this complaint which was made following September 10. But on that matter I think we are certainly entitled to know more. I do not believe any complaint worthy of the name was made with regard to him. As I say, the evidence of his record in the hotels is all against it.
The second question I asked was whether his salary had been reduced when he was sent to a smaller hotel, and the answer was no. I also asked what had been the salary of the previous manager and that information was refused. That is an interesting question because if, in fact, the Canadian National Railways business is carried on in such a way that the manager of a rather small hotel with 80 rooms gets the same salary as does the manager of one of the company's largest hotels in a western metropolis, with about three times as many rooms, then all I can say is that it is a curious way to carry on business; and I shall be greatly surprised if that is indeed the way business is carried on. I should be interested to know the answer- for I did not get an answer to this question as to what the previous manager's salary was-and whether it would not have shown that it was lower.
That thought raises in my mind this question, and it must raise it in the mind of every man in the house. If it is a fact-which I surmise, from just looking at the situation -that he was sent to a smaller hotel with the same salary which he would not ordinarily have got, then it looks to me as though there may have been a twinge of conscience and that after treating him in this disgraceful manner, in order to alleviate the matter a bit he was left on the same salary. That is surmised; nevertheless I think any reasonable man would make that surmise on the facts as I have brought them forward.
The Address-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell
The other question I asked and that I wish to refer to was this:
Was any complaint, verbal or written, regarding any incident at the Fort Garry hotel during the Prime Minister's visit on September 10 last, made to the railway or hotel management or to the Department of Transport, or to any representative of any of the foregoing by or on behalf of the Prime Minister or of any one of those who were accompanying him at Winnipeg on September 10 last?
The answer to that question appeared in rather a curious form. When I first received it, I took from it a meaning that, on further study, I think perhaps was not intended. I have read the question to you. It was not split up in any way. It was one question, just numbered "3". The answer goes like this:
3. No.
Then below that is written:
In so far as the Department of Transport is concerned:
And below that again is written:
3. No.
When I got that first I thought what it meant was that the Department of Transport was answering only for itself, and it was giving no answer as regards the railway company. But it has been suggested to me- and I think it accords with what Mr. Gordon himself has said, and I shall refer to that later-that that first "no" was intended to be a general "no" affecting my whole question. At any rate the matter is not of very great importance because Mr. Gordon has given a separate answer in which he says:
No complaint has been made either by the Prime Minister or on his behalf in respect to his recent visit at the Fort Garry.
These are Mr. Gordon's own words. If this matter is to be left here I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it leaves us all in a very unfortunate position. I believe that these answers have been given without a full knowledge of the facts. I do not believe it is possible to survey what has happened and to believe that what happened on November 12 or thereabouts had nothing to do with what happened on September 10, and I hope no one will try to say that was the case.
Some ingenious person makes a point regarding Mr. Gordon's statement which I have just read, and here I quote again from the Tribune. After saying that the hotel staff members emphasized that the complaints were not laid by Mr. St. Laurent, but by one or more members of his party, it goes on to say:
Gordon did not mention complaints by other members of the Prime Minister's party, which were reported by Tribune local and Ottawa sources.

The Address-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell
In other words, the suggestion is that Mr. Gordon's denial covered only the Prime Minister, but made no denial in so far as the members of the party were concerned. I will read it again:
No complaint has been made either by the Prime Minister or on his behalf in respect to his recent visit at the Fort Garry.
I think this was intended to cover the members of the party. Where does that leave us, Mr. Speaker? I suggest that no sane man will doubt that these two incidents were connected. To assume the opposite is to assume that the management of the Canadian National hotels are taking leave of their senses. It is to assume that an unworthy man, a man who did not know how to greet the Prime Minister, a man who did not know how to show proper consideration for the people who were travelling with the Prime Minister, was kept in the service of the company all these years and promoted from time to time.
I want to point out that the suggestion that he was in any way inefficient is contradicted in the strongest manner by the guests in the hotel themselves. I read again from the Tribune:
Permanent guests contacted today said they had no complaints about service which would reflect on Mr. Pitt's management.
All praised him as a valuable asset to the hotel.
Said one guest: "I have been here 12 years. I have never met a finer man. He is the essence of refinement and does his best for everyone, always. We feel very badly about the situation."
As I say, to assume that these two events are not connected is just to assume that we are living in a world of unreason where two and two do not make four. It is no wonder that the Tribune asks the following question in an editorial on November 13:
The Tribune's report of the dismissal of Robert S. Pitt from his position as manager of the Fort Garry hotel, and his subsequent transfer to Brandon, is chiefly important because of the one big question it raises in the public mind: Is there political interference in the management of the C.N.R. or its hotel system on the part of government functionaries close to the Prime Minister?
Then later:
Was Mr. Pitt given any kind of a fair trial? Were the complaints against him and his hotel investigated? There is no evidence that we have been able to uncover that the answer is in the affirmative to either of these questions. Rather, the answer seems to be that the hotel manager was removed from his job without proper investigation because someone in the government or close to the government had thundered. It will be a bad state of affairs for the Canadian National Railways if it is saddled with government interference in management.
1 want to ask you, Mr. Speaker, how this kind of thing can happen. We are not that kind of people. In this house we differ on many things, but 1 would say that this house


has a sense of fairness, and I believe that if all members were free to express their opinion they would agree with me that this is an obvious case of outrageous injustice. It is not possible to reach any other conclusion but that directly or indirectly there was pressure. That is what the Tribune says, and that is what I believe. We are not that kind of people. How does this kind of thing arise? I think it is clear that is arises when people have too much power for too long. They just begin to take themselves too seriously; they begin to throw their weight around. This is a lamentable situation, a distortion of the ordinary sense of fairness of the ordinary Canadian, just because he has got to the state where he is, I believe, throwing his weight about and taking himself too seriously.
This whole matter is far bigger than the Fort Garry hotel and Mr. Pitt. It raises the whole question not only of the Canadian National but of the use of power. I hope there will be such widespread indignation arise out of this that it will not be able to be hushed up, that it will be dealt with and that justice will be done. I hope the Legion will come to the rescue of this excellent officer. I hope the union, which has already earned our gratitude by bringing this matter out into the public, will press it; and I hope every fair-minded man will press it to the point that reparation is made, and made now, not months from now, when it is slithered into and nobody is looking, and there is no real reparation of the injustice because the man is still left under a cloud.
And finally, I put it up to the Prime Minister who was there. He, I believe, would have no patience with this kind of thing. I put it up to the Prime Minister that here is a case of injustice that should be remedied, not at some time remote from now, but now; and not in any hole in the comer fashion but in the open, so that everybody knows what has been done.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. Dickey (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in entering the debate at this time it is not with any intention of making a detailed report on the defence production program. It is both more convenient and more proper that such details be made available to hon. members through the report of the Department of Defence Production for the current fiscal year, through the special committee on defence expenditures, or when the estimates of the department are being considered by the house. On the other hand, it is approximately six months since the right hon. Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) spoke last in this house regarding this program and there have been significant developments since that time. These have occurred both in the field of raw materials and in our actual production and procurement programs.
Most hon. members will be aware that in recent months there has been a distinct improvement in the world supply of raw materials. Evidence of this is the fact that in the last six months the international materials conference has felt that the situation permitted them to disband the committees on pulp and paper, on wool, on cotton and on cotton linters. Furthermore they have decided that it will no longer be necessary to recommend the allocation of cobalt, tungsten and zinc.
Here in Canada we have continued our policy of releasing controls just as quickly as possible. On May 26 control orders on lead, zinc and cadmium were lifted. On September 9 the minister announced the sale of the Emerald tungsten mine to Canadian Explorations Limited. During the past year explorations by this company on its own mining claims established substantial additional quantities of tungsten ore, with the result that the Canadian position has eased.


On September 17 the minister also announced that control orders covering copper wire and rods, rod copper and copper alloys and aluminum had been lifted, making it no longer necessary for industry to submit their orders to the department for approval.
Order in council P. C. 4212, dated October 9, 1952, removed pulpwood and newsprint from the list of materials declared essential under the Defence Production Act. Those commodities had been declared essential, not for domestic reasons but in order to permit the government to implement allocations recommended by the international materials conference. When the pulp and paper committee of the international materials conference indicated that the necessity of allocating pulp and paper for strategic purposes no longer existed, the government removed those commodities from the essential list.
By order in council P. C. 4551, dated November 28, most of the chemicals which had been declared essential under the Defence Production Act were removed from that category. This again was initiated because increased production had brought the supply of these materials into balance with demand.
On November 17 the control order on sulphur was revoked. This has been made possible in part by the fact that in recent months the supply of sulphur in the United States has been slightly greater than demand, thus enabling authorities in that country to revoke their control order, and also due to the fact that sulphur-producing facilities recently established in Canada were getting into production.
These decontrol orders have, of course, been announced by the minister as quickly as decisions have been taken. However, I have reviewed them this evening.in order to emphasize that the government is in fact implementing its avowed policy to keep the control machinery of this country to the absolute minimum consistent with the requirements of our defence effort. On the other hand, as the world's foremost exporter of many of these materials, we have a serious responsibility to our allies to make the greatest possible contribution to their essential requirements. Consequently we must keep the supply of these strategic materials under constant review, and this will be done.
We shall continue also to encourage increased Canadian production. All that need be said in this connection is that expansion programs undertaken by our major primary producers are progressing satisfactorily.
One of the essential materials over which we have had to exercise control has been steel, but there are now indications of improvement in the steel supply. Our Canadian industry has been producing steadily at

high levels, and steel production in the United States has recovered quickly from last summer's work stoppage.
Last month a new steel finishing mill came into production at Sault Ste. Marie which will give us an additional 250,000 tons of rolled steel products annually. In addition new facilities came into production this week at Hamilton which will add 650,000 tons of steel ingots a year to our present production. However, in spite of this increase in Canadian production the demand for steel is growing steadily, so we expect to maintain our level of imports from the United States, the United Kingdom and other countries.
It has been the policy during the past two years to control production and distribution of steel in order to make sure that direct defence needs were met first, but always with minimum disruption of normal commercial practices. With the prospect of improved supplies in 1953 the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) now feels justified in revoking, effective December 31 of this year, order SD-2 which prohibits less essential construction. Inventory limitations contained in order SD-1 will also be rescinded effective on the same date.
However, it will still be necessary to exercise control over steel distribution in order to ensure that defence requirements are met. Although we can look forward to continued improvement in general steel supplies during the coming months, it must be emphasized that some specific forms and types of steel probably will be in relatively short supply for some time to come, particularly steel plate and structural steel. Therefore the easing of steel restrictions in accordance with these announcements does not mean that ample supplies will be available immediately for all uses.
May I now turn to the production side of our defence program. As you know, Mr. Speaker, in this period of uncertainty our aim has been threefold; first, to produce the equipment needed to meet our international commitments and to defend our own country; second, to provide the productive facilities required to enable this country to swing into full-scale production should the need arise; and third, to build a strong economy that can supply the raw materials, the plant and equipment needed to sustain the Canadian economy in the event of an all-out war.
In addressing the house last spring the minister pointed out that, in the production of military equipment, the first year of the defence program was a period of preparation and organization, and that in the second year we would see actual deliveries and completed facilities. Although there are still another
The Address-Mr. Dickey four months to go in this fiscal year, production has definitely started to roll in all phases of the program. In some parts of the program most of the deliveries have been made. In others volume production is just getting under way. Where items are procured from regular commercial production it is comparatively easy to fill the requirements of the Department of National Defence. Where complicated military weapons of new design are produced, the story naturally is different.
A critical examination of the defence pro

duction program indicates that neither government nor industry fully appreciated the complexity of the job of producing to the exacting requirements of modern warfare, requirements which are not less difficult as specifications are constantly varied to take advantage of the newest technological advances. It is now necessary to guard against obsolescence even before production is under way. Canada has no monopoly on these problems. We know that they are showing up in the United States and the United Kingdom. They are no doubt harassing other countries including, we hope, the U.S.S.R.
Part of the problem is that we are working in entirely new fields and often with new materials. The use of jet propulsion in aircraft is something we had never tackled before. Here we have to produce an engine weighing over a ton that is capable of 8,000 revolutions per minute. In shipbuilding more aluminum is being used in place of wood and steel, and this requires the development of new skills and techniques. High stress factors in modern aircraft have necessitated the use of forged components in place of fabricated parts. High tensile castings introduce new and exacting metallurgical requirements. On the precision side we find that whereas during the last war we spoke of tolerances of a thousandth of an inch, today we talk of a ten-thousandth of an inch.
Despite these problems we are making good progress. We have already delivered intricate equipment in some volume to the three armed services. Before the end of this fiscal year there will be a sharp rise in deliveries. It is important to note that much of this production will be flowing from Canadian facilities that did not exist eighteen months ago. All hon. members are aware of the tremendous strides made by Canadian industry during the last war and of the capital expansion that * has taken place since that time. This broadening and diversification of our industrial base was invaluable when we started the present defence program. However, because of recent developments in modern armament design, and because we wanted to make more parts and components

In other cases accelerated depreciation has been granted to take care of some of the risk involved, or we have stepped in and supplied, on the basis of government ownership, the plant or machine tools required.
The establishment of these facilities is a major part of our defence production program. There has been careful examination of the fields in which, for economic or strategic reasons, production in Canada was warranted, and we have then taken steps to ensure that facilities were established not only to meet current requirements but also to take care of accelerated production in an all-out effort.
This evening I want to mention some of these new facilities that are actually in production. The major part of this development has been in the aircraft industry. Two years ago the government purchased a site at Malton and entered into a contract with A. V. Roe for the design and construction of a crown-owned jet engine plant. This plant has now been built. The tools and equipment were obtained partly from the original A. V. Roe plant where the first Orendas were made, but mainly from a variety of sources in stiff competition with aircraft manufacturers of other countries. Much of the equipment had to be specially designed to meet new manufacturing techniques. Not only will this plant meet our immediate requirements, but it is capable of making a valuable contribution to meet expanded production needs. Orenda engines in substantial numbers are now coming off the production line, not only to power the CF-100 but also for the F-86 Sabre, which will greatly improve the performance of that aircraft.
We are now making more of the parts and *components for airframes and aero engines than at any time in our history. We have set up a plant that is producing fuel systems for the Orenda, while another is making combustion chambers. We now have plants that are manufacturing blades for jet engines. These blades, which are like small wings, must be forged, machined and finally ground to a tolerance of two-thousandths of an inch. A new Canadian plant is now producing, from a special heat-resisting alloy, castings and rings to be used in the hot end of a jet engine where temperatures reach 1,300 degrees fahrenheit. There were some people who thought we would be unable to produce in Canada the magnesium casting needed for


the jet program. These castings are now being turned out in quantity.
The high speeds attainable in jet aircraft have increased the stresses on the airframe and this, together with greater military loads, has increased the weight. To get the highest possible efficiency we have had to go to great lengths to produce refined structures. In the F-86 Sabre the main wing skin is formed from a sheet three-eighths of an inch thick, and we now have equipment in Canada which can machine this sheet in such a way that it tapers in thickness from five-sixteenths to one-sixteenth of an inch over the fifteen feet of its length. This operation is controlled to within three-thousandths of an inch.
We now have other plants that are producing undercarriage components, gear boxes, radomes, propellers, flexible hose assemblies, and filters. All this adds up to a much greater degree of self-sufficiency in our Canadian aircraft industry.
In the shipbuilding field, facilities have been set up to produce gears and naval auxiliary equipment. A new naval turbine plant, as modern as any of its type in the world, is now making complete sets of propulsion machinery for our escort vessels.
In guns and ammunition, most of the developments have been within the various divisions of Canadian Arsenals Limited. As most hon. members know, most of these divisions were kept in a stand-by condition after the second world war. In reactivating these plants we rehabilitated some of the machinery in storage and augmented this with new machine tools where necessary.
Our capacity to produce explosives has been steadily expanding. The de Salaberry plant at Valleyfield has been completely rehabilitated and put into operation by Defence Industries (1951) Limited, a subsidiary of Canadian Industries Limited. About two months ago, as was announced by the minister, Canadian Arsenals took over that plant as a producing unit.
These are some of the new facilities that have been created in the last two years. In some instances it has meant breaking sod and building and equipping new plants. In other cases it has meant the installation of additional machine tools in plants already in production. Since the department was set up in April, 1951, the department has ordered some 4,000 machine tools valued at approximately $35 million. Despite the long lead time on deliveries, over 2,700 of these machines had been installed in Canadian plants by October of this year. This was in addition to the rehabilitated crown-owned tools held in storage since the last war and now allocated to defence industries.

These facilities, now in production, are not only the basis of our preparedness effort but they also form the nucleus of an all-out effort if war is forced upon us. Of equal importance, those facilities will, if international conditions permit, make an important contribution to our over-all economy.
I have been speaking of two aspects of the defence program-the production of weapons and equipment to meet our current needs and the building up of facilities as insurance against an all-out emergency. To keep the over-all program in perspective, I would like to deal briefly with a third part of the program which I mentioned earlier-the importance of a strong economy and a broad industrial base as a defence against possible aggression in the future.
In the last few years we have achieved record levels of production, income and employment. What is particularly significant from a defence standpoint is the economic expansion that has taken place in those segments of the Canadian economy that would bear the brunt of full mobilization. Over-all capital investment has been maintained at a very high rate in very recent years but, since Korea, there has been a definite change in its composition. To meet the demands of defence, we have seen a marked increase in the expansion of basic industrial capacity and a corresponding shift away from investment in consumer goods and services. This means that we are now able to manufacture more iron and steel products; to make more electrical apparatus; and to produce a wider variety of chemical products than we ever could before. We have, at the same time, been building up our power potential and expanding along other lines that would provide the necessary base for large-scale military production.
In the field of international co-operation there has been continued progress in strengthening the defences of the free world. In our relationship with the United States a number of steps have been taken to enable our two countries to co-operate more fully in our joint defence effort. Last February we signed an agreement which simplifies and co-ordinates procedures on defence contracts, and provides a more satisfactory basis on which our two governments can do business. Another agreement on security makes it possible for Canada and the United States to exchange information pertaining to defence production with a minimum of delay and red tape.

The most effective use of the resources of both Canada and the United States is essential to the success of the defence effort. Several months ago, when Canadian orders in the United States were about twice as high as those placed in this country, the minister pointed out that there would be an increase in United States orders and a levelling off in Canadian purchases. This is now taking place. There has been a very marked increase in United States contracts placed in this country. In the 1951-52 United States fiscal year, they totalled more than $325 million. During the same period, Canadian orders amounted to about $279 million. As our own facilities have come into production it has been possible to ease up on the heavy initial purchases that had to be made in the United States to get our defence program under way.
On the other hand, our defence purchases in the United Kingdom are increasing. In the fiscal year 1950-51, Canadian government defence orders placed in the United Kingdom amounted to $8 million. In the fiscal year 1951-52 they were about $38 million. In the first seven months of this fiscal year, orders placed are worth about $55 million.
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to prolong this statement. Summarizing briefly, the strategic materials situation is improving and we are taking advantage of this circumstance to relax controls as quickly as the requirements of the defence effort permit. Significant quantities of complicated equipment are now being made available to the armed services, and deliveries will increase sharply before the end of the fiscal year. An impressive framework of new facilities has been established in the last two years and forms the real basis of our defence effort. Finally, the Canadian economy is being maintained at a record level, providing us not only with a strong bulwark against communism but also providing our fellow Canadians with the highest standard of living in our history.

I should like, Mr. Speaker, to speak for a few moments about the forced retirement of Brigadier A. B. Connelly, the brilliant young officer who was fired to make a scapegoat for this government's fiasco in dealing with the Koje island incident. I happened to be a classmate of Brigadier Connelly's for four years at the Koyal Military College, between 1927 and 1931. During four years such as that, you get to know a great deal about a man's character and ability. I believe that all those who were associated with Brigadier Connelly at that time were convinced that he was one of the brightest, cleverest, ablest cadets that ever came out of that institution. As the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) pointed out the other day, since his graduation his whole career has been one of rapid promotion to some of the highest jobs in the army.
I have known very well a great many of the men who, right up until the time he was fired, were associated with Brigadier Connelly in his work. I also know a great many of the men who have worked for him. They are all of the opinion that he would have risen to the very top of the tree.
What was the great mistake that Brigadier Connelly is supposed to have made? It is simply that he reported as a routine matter, instead of by high priority cable, the fact that one company of infantry from our 25th brigade was under consideration for guard


duty on Koje island. I believe that any soldier would have acted in exactly the same manner as Brigadier Connelly acted, because to soldiers the use of one company for temporary guard duty is a routine matter, and not a matter requiring high government decision.
If all our senior officers are going to have to know how to solve the eccentricities of the Liberal political mind in the future, there is no doubt about it that they are all going to require a very special course in this very inexact subject. I believe it is putting far too heavy a responsibility on men whose job it is to direct our fighting forces in the field.
I want now to deal very briefly with another matter that the hon. member for Nanaimo brought up when speaking in this house on December 1. He referred to the fact that in future the time spent at educational institutions would be considered as service time when working out pensions for commissioned officers in our armed forces. As he pointed out, that is a very just and desirable provision. I believe it is also necessary that officers who have already been commissioned should also be able to count the time spent at educational institutions as service time when computing the pension which they will receive. I believe this is a very necessary provision which the government should consider. I sincerely hope that in the near future the government will extend the present regulation to make that possible.

Mr. Speaker, although I came to the house in the fall of 1949, I am speaking for the first time tonight. The task entrusted to me by my electors is crystal clear: they have sent me here to support the government. I might add that the decision of the electors of Laurier was practically unanimous, because the Progressive Conservative party, aware of the people's wishes, did not contest the riding. The C.C.F. party followed suit. My only opponent was a member of the Labour-Progressive party who polled only a few hundred votes and he succeeded in doing so only by omitting, as much as possible, to mention the name of his party in the constituency.
I am confident of having fulfilled my mandate without having to interfere with the government's policy, the trend of which has not changed since 1949.
In 1949, the electors of the constituency of Laurier, like those in all parts of Canada, expressed their confidence in the Liberal party because it has worked towards a united, a sovereign and prosperous Canada, whose citizens were already enjoying a high degree of security.

In 1949-need I recall an event so vividly remembered by our people, so burning a memory for our opponents-Canadians from coast to coast chose the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent as head of the nation.
This choice was not to be regretted. Under the Liberal regime, Canada has constantly strengthened her unity, her sovereignty, her prosperity and the security of her people. Incidentally, the Conservatives, who, since the last election in the United States, take pleasure in identifying themselves with the Republicans-thus labouring under quite a delusion -should remember that all the largest magazines and newspapers in that country who supported the Republican party have, especially during the past year, praised the financial and economic development of Canada as well as her increasing prosperity. Several of them have even expressed the wish that their country be governed by men like those who make up the present government.
During the electoral campaign of 1949 our opponents, indulging in some wishful thinking, had predicted that the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent would resign immediately following the election.
To the satisfaction of my constituents, as well as of the whole country, and to their good fortune, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent is still the leader of the Liberal party and of the government. For all, he remains the man of the whole nation. It is not mere gallantry to point out too that the first lady of this country is still today Mrs. Louis St. Laurent.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to pay tribute to my predecessor, the Hon. Ernest Bertrand who, for fourteen years, so fittingly represented the constituency of Montreal Laurier. His constituents were honoured with his cabinet appointment, he having been originally Minister of Fisheries and latterly Postmaster General. The electors of Montreal Laurier think of him with gratitude and their admiration for his career remains undimmed in spite of his present removal from the public scene due to his appointment to the bench.
The support given to the government by my constituency is as assured today as it was in 1949; and it is equally strong in all parishes. Hence I did not have to voice any protest when it was substantially modified during the last redistribution.
I have but one regret, and it is to be deprived of a considerable portion of the people who placed confidence in me on my first election, as well as of organizers and devoted friends who never spared me their support. With the general elections coming, our opponents fill the air with their election-inspired statements. Hence, so much talk about health insurance.
It is not surprising that our socialists are sponsoring a new social security program; they would like it so very much if all our citizens were to depend on a state which they expect to run some day. Yet if they succeeded in nationalizing everything, in accordance with their policy, the plight of this country would be such that each citizen would have to rely on the state for his daily bread.
However, when we see the Tories, who, as a matter of principle, have always opposed social security measures, we must come to the conclusion that they are tired of being in opposition and that they have decided to abandon their principles and forget their past in an effort to assume power.
In requesting the implementation of a health insurance scheme, our opponents are merely showing their approval for legislation which the Liberal government will bring down in due course.
On the other hand it is noteworthy that any sound proposals which could be found in our opponents' platforms at any given time have sooner or later been put into effect by the Liberals.
In my opinion, before embarking on a health insurance scheme, we must first expand and increase our hospital facilities, sanatoriums and other medical institutions.
Before permitting a larger number of people to enter those institutions, we must provide the required accommodation and increase the necessary facilities.
Before calling the ambulance, one must ascertain that a bed is available in the hospital.
Therefore, it is a sound policy of the government to implement its health plan step by step.
Besides the sick there are the disabled. A sick man might be deprived for a few days, a few weeks or a few months of the income necessary to support himself and the members of his family. The disabled, on the contrary, might be deprived of these means for the rest of their lives. The sick person has to face considerable expenses for various lengths of time. The crippled would probably have to incur during their lifetime expenses resulting from their infirmities.

The Address-Mr. Lefrangois
Remarkable work is now being done in Canada towards the rehabilitation of the disabled, especially among the veterans. Amazing results are being achieved.
However a large proportion of crippled people will never be in a position to rehabilitate themselves. A few years ago the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand) suggested the implementation of a special allowance plan in their favour. While congratulating him for having thus focused the government's attention on their plight, may I, in turn, express the wish that, when the time has come to set up a national health insurance plan, some consideration will also be given to invalids.
We already have pensions for the blind. Still there are any number of other ailments which beset a large number of our citizens. Crippled in body, they barely manage to exist while their dependents remain in miserable circumstances.
If there is one case where private charity is unequal to the task, that is it. I am convinced that the whole nation would enthusiastically approve of the adoption of a plan calling for allowances for crippled persons.
I am also satisfied that my party, which has so rapidly brought up the standard of living of the people of this country, will see to it that our crippled citizens are assured of that measure of comfort and security to which everyone is entitled in a truly civilized country.
Before closing these remarks, I should like to congratulate both the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They have expressed the opinion and feelings of the great majority of Canadians.
It is with great pleasure that I listened to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi, whom I learned to know and appreciate during the course of his electoral campaign. The house has had occasion to realize the fluency with which he can express himself in both languages.
In closing my remarks, I should like to express the hope that the government, after having gratified us with such a perfect loudspeaker system, will favour us with a system of simultaneous translation which would allow everyone to hear all the speeches in his own language, regardless of the one used by the speaker. I am convinced that such an innovation would make for better understanding between all members of the house.

Mr. Speaker, before the vote is taken on this amendment to the amendment I wish to say a few words-and I assure the house that I will not detain it long-to explain why the C.C.F. group can and will vote for this subamendment. I wish to read the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) yesterday afternoon. It reads:
That the amendment be amended by adding at the end thereof the following:
" (f) To bring before this house for adoption, a realistic financial and economic policy that will ensure the orderly development of Canada's resources, guarantee adequate markets at remunerative prices to producers, and provide to every Canadian his just share of the wealth our resources can be made to yield."
If I could have had the time to do so, Mr. Speaker, I should have liked to read part of the speech made by the hon. member for Lethbridge this afternoon. I may be just as stupid as he says I am-[DOT] and really I am not worrying about it very much; I am getting too old for that-but if I were as much at sea on economic matters as the hon. member for Lethbridge is, I certainly would worry.
I said that the C.C.F. would vote for this subamendment and why. As a matter of fact, I believe we are the only party in this house that can logically and conscientiously vote for this subamendment. of Hansard. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked this question:

speechtext: Would you do away with welfare legislation? . . .

I would like to answer the hon. gentleman's question if I may. It has always been found that you cannot readily retract or undo something the country has already done.
What does that mean? It means that he would like to do away, as quickly as it possibly can be done, with our social legislation. He would like to remove from the statute books of Canada all the social legislation that is on them. I continue with the quotation:
-but I would say that the greatest welfare that can come to the people is to leave with them their absolute freedom to act according to their own conscience and will.
Well, if you are going to leave them to their absolute freedom to act according to their own consciences, why bring in a financial and economic policy that will ensure the orderly development of Canada's resources? Why bring in a financial and economic policy that will guarantee adequate markets at remunerative prices to producers, and why bring in a financial and economic policy that will provide to every Canadian his just share of the wealth our resources can be made to yield? All the things they are asking for in this subamendment require planning, planning on a large scale. Who is to say what each individual's just share is? Is that to be left to a matter of chance? And if it is left to a matter of chance, what chance has the weak to get his share in competition with the strong? Did anyone ever hear of anything quite so fantastic or statements so much at variance with each other as the statement made by the hon. member for Macleod on December 1 and the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Lethbridge on December 10?
